text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
British naval officer SIR JAMES BREMER was born in 1786.
Australian poet MARY HANNAY FOOTT was born in 1846. She wrote "Where the Pelican Builds" after two Queensland pastoralists went missing while seeking western pastures.

The Australian broadcasting executive ALFRED BENNETT, who opened Radio 2GB, was born in 1889. He said "we have no right to use wireless unless we utilise it for the Nation's uplift and progress". He was a Mussolini fan and formed the right-wing "Who's For Australia League".

American composer GEORGE GERSHWIN, who composed some of the most enduring popular music ever written, was born in 1898. He wrote "Rhapsody in Blue" in 1924, "An American in Paris" in 1928, and many popular musicals and songs. His brother IRA GERSHWIN wrote many of the lyrics GEORGE's compositions such as "I Got Rhythm" and "Embraceable You". The 1931 collaboration between the brothers "Of Thee I Sing" was the first musical to win a Pulitizer Prize.

Australian actor LEONARD TEALE, whose career covered theatre, radio and television, was born in 1922. He died in 1994 near his Sydney home after collapsing on a harbour-side walking track. He gained prominence for his radio character of Superman. He later starred in the Australian-made television series "Homicide" and "Seven Little Australians".
Australian cricketer IAN CHAPPELL was born in 1943. One of the cricketing CHAPPELL brothers who gave years of service to the Australian team.
British pop singer, pianist and composer BRYAN FERRY, who was lead singer of 'Roxy Music', was born in 1945.

Australian singer OLIVIA NEWTON-JOHN, was born in England in 1948. She gained prominence on the Australian rock Television series "Bandstand" and went on to international stardom. In addition to her albums OLIVIA starred in the movie "Grease" with JOHN TRAVOLTA, and hosted an animal series in Australia called Wildlife.
** EVENTS **
1815 : The Holy Alliance was signed by Tsar ALEXANDER I
of Russia, FRANCIS I of Austria and FREDERICK WILLIAM III, King of Prussia.
1820 : American frontiersman DANIEL BOONE died. He paved

the way for the first western migrattion of settlers. During the American revolution he led militias against Indians allied with the British. When he was captured by the Shawnee war party he so impressed the chief that he was adopted by the tribe. He left the Indians and continued westward.
1901 : The first America's Cup race was held.
1907 : New Zealand became a Dominion. At an impressive

ceremony at Wellington's Parliament House the country had its status raised from a colony to a Dominion. Reports of the day said the Governor-general LORD PLUNKET stepped forward and read out the King's proclamation before handing it to the Prime Minister SIR JOSEPH WARD. After three cheers for the King the Maoris stepped in and danced a an ear-splitting haka.
1937 : The Empress of the Blues, BESSIE SMITH, died from

loss of blood after a car accident in Mississippi. There were claims that had MISS SMITH been white she wouldn't have died. Friends said she bled to death because the ambulance deliberately didn't hurry to the "black accident". She began singing in a gospel church in Tennessee and recorded her first record for "black communities" in 1923.
1943 : A secret team of 14 Australians sank or damaged

seven Japanese ships in Singapore. The Z special force sailed a former Japanese fishing ketch, the "Krait" from Exmouth Gulf in Western Australia, posing as a Javanese trader. Six members in three canoes struck, attaching limpet mines to ships without being detected. The "Krait" was intercepted once on the return journey but not inspected. The mission was one of the most successful of the second World War.
1957 : The first performance of the BERNSTEIN-SONDHEIM
musical "West Side Story" was given in New York.
1978 : The Australian government announced it would give two Northern Territory Aboriginal tribes title to 95,000 square miles of land.
1983 : An Australian yacht won the America's Cup, taking

the cup away from the New York Yacht Club for the first time in 132 years. On a day most Australians will remember ALAN BOND's "Australia II" defeated the US yacht "Liberty" in the last of seven races off Newport, Rhode Island. Australian Prime Minister at the time, BOB HAWKE, joined in the national celebration at the victory and uttered that memorable quote "Any boss who sacks someone for not tunring up today is a bum". "Australia II" was skippered by JOHN BERTRAND, while DENNIS CONNER skippered "Liberty".
1984 : Britain and China agreed that Hong Kong would
revert to Chinese rule when the lease expires in 1997.
1985 : The British government allocated one million
pounds to counter the spread of Aids.
1989 : The last Vietnamese troops pulled out of Cambodia.
1994 : An outbreak of the plague was reported in the
western Indian city of Surat. Four days later the plague had spread to the capital New Delhi and international tourists were warned to stay away from the country.
